BEFORE YOU HIRE AN AI DEVELOPMENT COMPANY, ASK THIS.

You’ve seen the demo.
The AI looks impressive.
The proposal promises a fast launch.

But before you sign the contract, ask yourself:
“Do I really know what I’m buying?”

Choosing the wrong AI development partner can mean months of delays, unexpected costs, security risks, and a product that never makes it into production.

Before signing, make sure your potential partner can clearly answer:
- What business outcome will AI improve?
Not “AI transformation.” Ask for a specific metric—revenue, retention, support cost, conversion, or productivity.

- Who owns my data, code and AI assets?
Your contract should clearly cover source code, models, prompts, datasets, infrastructure and IP.

- How will you prove the AI actually works?
Ask about evaluation datasets, accuracy thresholds, testing and human review—not just a demo.

- What happens when the AI gets it wrong?
Production AI needs fallback mechanisms, confidence thresholds, human escalation and monitoring.

- How will it integrate with my existing systems?
CRM, ERP, databases, APIs and authentication often become the real development challenge.

- Who is actually building my product?
Meet the engineers. Understand their experience, roles and availability—not just the sales team.

- How will my data stay secure?
Ask where data is processed, who can access it, how it is stored, and what compliance standards are followed.

- What happens after launch?
AI isn't “build once and forget.” Models, prompts, data and user behavior change continuously.

Upwork Isn't Dying. It's Firing Its Smallest Clients. Here's What That Means For You.

I read something last week that changed how I look at Upwork.
An analyst wrote: "Upwork isn't losing clients. It's firing them."
And the data backs it up.

Here's what's actually happening:
Active clients have dropped for 8 consecutive quarters. From 868,000 in Q2 2024 to 763,000 in Q2 2026.

Sounds like a dying marketplace, right?

Wrong.

Because spending per client hit a record $5,230 - up 5% year-over-year, and it's risen for 8 straight quarters.

The clients who are leaving? They're the small, low-complexity, low-ticket customers. The ones who used to post $50 jobs. The ones AI is eating.
The clients who are staying? They're spending more. On bigger, more complex projects.

What does this mean for you?
Upwork is becoming a high-value, AI-driven platform. And the freelancers who win will be the ones who adapt.

But there's a problem.
Problem 1: Most freelancers are still competing for work that's disappearing.
Short, repeatable, low-complexity tasks? AI is automating them. Upwork's own CEO said AI "degraded the volume of client activity on the low end, impacting contracts of $500 and below".

Problem 2: Ghost jobs are draining Connects.
Clients face zero penalties for letting a job post die. Freelancers spend Connects, get nothing, and no refunds are issued.
One 13-year veteran with $100K+ earned said: "I saw a 102 Connects bid for a single job. This is no longer a marketplace. It's a gambling den."

Problem 3: Uma AI decides who gets seen.
In May 2026, Upwork eliminated Specialized Profiles. Now, Uma - Upwork's AI - decides which freelancers get highlighted "for every client and every opportunity".

If your profile is vague or generic, Uma can't categorize you. And if Uma can't categorize you, clients never see you.

So what do you actually do?

Three things that work right now:
1. Stop being a generalist.
"Web Developer | Designer | SEO Expert" confuses the AI. Pick one niche. Get specific. Clarity beats talent when the gatekeeper is an algorithm.

2. Treat every Connect like it's your last.
Check the client's hiring history - not just the "payment verified" badge. If they have 0 hires and the job looks too good to be true, skip it.

3. Build proof outside the platform.
High-ticket clients Google your name before they hire you. Your off-platform presence is now your competitive advantage.

The uncomfortable truth:
Upwork isn't broken. It's changing. And the freelancers who adapt first are the ones who win.

Still applying to everything? Shifted to a positioning-first strategy? Or figuring it out as you go?

One thing I've started paying more attention to is whether a decision is reversible.
Some decisions are difficult to undo.
Others aren't.
Hiring a new executive is different from testing a new workflow for two weeks.
Building an entire AI infrastructure is different from running a small pilot.
Signing a long-term contract is different from trying a new supplier on a limited basis.
Yet organizations sometimes treat all decisions as if they require the same level of commitment.
They don't.
For reversible decisions, speed and learning can matter more.
For irreversible decisions, slowing down can be valuable.
This sounds simple.
But it changes the question a leader asks.
Instead of:
“How confident are we?”
sometimes ask:
“How costly would it be to change our mind?”
If changing your mind is cheap, you may not need perfect information.
If changing your mind is expensive, you probably need much more thought before committing.
Good strategy isn't about avoiding uncertainty.
It's about understanding the cost of being wrong.

Without a digital negotiation layer that can instantly evaluate these trade-offs, the team defaults to the slowest, most expensive option out of fear of a compliance violation.

Another trend reshaping the field is the integration of cybersecurity into the supply chain data pipeline. In 2025, the most disruptive attacks were not on the warehouse management system itself, but on the sensor data feeding the predictive maintenance models. If your inventory optimization algorithm is relying on data from a compromised sensor, your "optimal" reorder point is actually a liability. The teams that are pulling ahead are embedding anomaly detection directly into the data ingestion layer, not just at the network perimeter.

The human-machine collaboration piece is also more nuanced than most believe. I have seen planners successfully delegate routine exception handling to AI agents, but only when the agent is trained on the specific trade-off preferences of that planner, not a generic company policy. When the agent can explain why it chose to expedite one shipment over another using the planner's own historical reasoning, trust accelerates rapidly.

For recruiters and hiring managers: the candidate you need is not the person who can run a standard ERP module or build a single forecast model. You need someone who can design the contract-aware data pipelines that make multimodal switching viable, who understands how to model cybersecurity risk as a supply chain variable, and who can build the feedback loops that align AI agents with human decision-making. I used Postman for 18 months. Thought I was doing API testing. Then a senior interviewer asked me one question. I had no answer.
 
"How do you validate that your API hasn't broken its contract with 3 downstream consumers?"
 
I said: "I'd check the response in Postman."
 
He nodded. Interview ended shortly after.
 
That failure taught me what API testing actually means at a senior level.

What juniors answer:

Send request → check status code → check response body

What seniors answer:

Contract validation across consumers
Schema drift detection
State injection to remove UI dependency
Mocking downstream failures to test resilience
Performance degradation thresholds, not just pass or fail
 
The difference isn't tools. It's the questions you know to ask before writing a single test.
 
Postman is where API exploration begins. Not where API testing ends.
 
It's the mindset shift most SDETs take years to make.

1. "Revenue is growing, but margin is dying. What do you do?"
Skip the generic "cut marketing" response. Break down SKU-level unit economics, eliminate cannibalizing promotions, and rationalize the tail end of your assortment.

2. "How do you negotiate with strategic US suppliers?"
Stop haggling over unit price. Negotiate Total Cost of Ownership (TCO), payment terms that free up working capital, and rebate brackets tied to performance.

3. "How do you de-risk a critical category?"
Single-source reliance is operational negligence. Map geographic exposure, build multi-origin redundancy, and set dynamic buffer stocks before disruptions hit.

4. "Cost vs. quality: which wins?"
A 5% procurement cut that drives a 10% return rate is net-negative. Protect the core customer touchpoints; strip operational waste downstream.

5. "How do you use analytics to move the needle?"
Dashboards are useless without commercial execution. Focus on inventory turn velocity, shelf incrementality, and price elasticity.

6. "Tell me about challenging senior leadership."
Remove ego and opinion. Bring clean data, model the financial trade-offs, and frame your recommendation around bottom-line EBITDA.

7. "Keep or kill a product line?"
Evaluate sales velocity, GMROI, and true basket contribution. If a SKU doesn't generate incremental value or customer acquisition, retire it.

8. "Where does AI actually fit into category management?"
Look past generative hype. Use machine learning for demand sensing, anomaly detection in rogue spend, and automated reorder triggers.

9. "How do you lead cross-functionally without direct authority?"
Influence is built on alignment, not title. Tie every team’s success metrics directly to category health and maintain absolute transparency.

10. "Your first 90 days?"
• Days 1–30: Audit inventory, spend data, and vendor contracts.
• Days 31–60: Target quick margin leakages and pilot low-risk optimizations.
• Days 61–90: Present a prioritized, numbers-backed roadmap that ties directly to revenue goals.

---

The Golden Rule: Never end an answer without stating the financial impact—margin saved, working capital unlocked, or risk prevented.

BofA was a customer of The Career Conversation for a number of years, so I have been following their news for a while and this article on Reuters showcases a potential new approach to entry level hiring for the banking sector in the AI era.

They have just committed to hiring 1,000 additional apprentices over the next two years, which is on top of the 800-plus it already brings in every year across Consumer Banking, Technology, Operations and other client-facing areas.

It's also putting US$150m over five years into workforce development organisations, building on the US$40m it already invested in 2025 through partnerships with more than 100 universities and community colleges and over 600 non-profits.

Of particular note, the apprenticeship pathway doesn't require a four-year degree, something I think we need to see a lot more of. 

This early careers hiring story is very counter to the p(doom) AI zeitguiest that is filling my feed at the moment and maybe an approach for others to consider, especially the lack of a four year degree. 

I am not suggesting this fixes the early careers AI conundrum, but I think this helps younger workers who feel the social contract has been broken. They can see a pathway to a stable job without the debt-carry of a degree.  A doorway in to work that runs on skills and not on certificates might be exactly the opening this moment needs more of. 

Brian Moynihan, BofA's CEO, put the reasoning plainly. "This is one more way for us to do what we can to help create a skilled American workforce for tomorrow."

Two more numbers of note from the release, both bank-wide rather than specific to the apprenticeship programme: a $50,000 minimum salary, and roughly 40% of BofA's overall hires don't hold a bachelor's degree.

The AI boom isn't being built by coders. It's being built by Electricians and HVAC Techs!!

We all talk about AI as if it lives in the cloud, some ethereal fantasy place up in the sky. It doesn't. It lives in concrete, copper and cooling systems, and someone has to build it, service it, maintain it and eventually, replace/upgrade it.

Australia's Powering Skills Organisation estimates the country needs an additional 72,000 electricians, technicians and related tradespeople by 2030. Data centres are a massive part of that demand, and they're fighting for the same workers as housing, renewables and general infrastructure. Any Recruiter working in this sector will attest to the struggle finding people in these trades.

Seek's AI Gauge report found that construction and site management ads tied to data centres now outnumber IT ads for the same sector. The biggest hiring need in the AI economy isn't software engineers. It's high-voltage electricians, HVAC technicians and commissioning specialists.

That creates a real bottle neck. Every electrician on a hyperscale build is one fewer available to work on a new home, and vice versa. Industry bodies like HIA and NECA have already flagged that the pipeline isn't keeping pace.

Two things stand out to me:
The bottleneck is skills, not capital. The money is there. The pipeline of qualified people isn't, and apprenticeship completion rates and an ageing workforce make that a slow problem to fix.

We're probably overlooking people who could transition. Someone with commercial, or industrial experience often has skills that could transition well to data centre work, but a CV keyword filter will never surface that. Skills need to be assessed on what someone can actually do, not just the job title on paper.(Prism Platform can help with this)

The businesses that win this race won't just be the ones with the best sites and power contracts, advantageous as that might be. They'll be the ones who find, train and keep the right people.

I have been having the same conversations for months.

With people across the corporate affairs industry considering their next career move.

With hiring managers and leaders looking ahead to 2027, asking what their function looks like today, what it needs to look like next, and planning for that now.

None of us has all the answers.

Two questions keep coming up.

1. It's nearly October. Is it realistic to secure and accept a new position before the end of the year?

Some argue yes. Others no.

I think it absolutely can happen.

The market isn't dead, and roles are still progressing.

If you're looking, I wouldn't take your foot off the pedal simply because we're heading into the final quarter of 2026.

2. What role will agency recruiters who support corporate affairs hiring play in 2027?

Such a great question and one that deserves its own post!

Agency recruiters will always have an important role in corporate affairs resourcing. This I am 100% sure of.

But I think we're going to see a bigger divide between those who thrive and those who don't.

Those who stay ahead will have genuine depth in their markets.

Trust and credibility. Networks that are actually networks, not databases.

Visible expertise and thought leadership.

And, I think most importantly above everything else, a willingness to rethink how recruitment is delivered.

The traditional recruitment model shouldn't automatically be the answer to every resourcing problem.

Executive search firms, for example, have traditionally operated largely on retainers. I'm not debating whether that's right or wrong.

I'm asking does every assignment need to look the same? I don't think it does.

Maybe a client needs a complete end to end market mapping and search.

Maybe they need support with only part of the process.

Maybe they need access to talent they can't reach themselves.

Maybe interim, contract or fractional expertise makes more sense than permanent headcount.

Maybe the fee should reflect the actual work required rather than automatically being a percentage of someone's remuneration.

And maybe AI can do some of the process while the recruiter focuses on judgement, relationships, context and trust.

I'm already experimenting with some of this in my own business.

Different ways of structuring searches.
Different ways of accessing specialist talent.
Different ways of thinking about what a "recruitment assignment" even needs to look like.

I'm not giving ALL my secrets away. 😏

But I firmly believe recruiters who can offer flexible, mixed resourcing solutions will stay ahead.

Not every organisation has the same problem.
Not every role requires the same solution.

And not every recruitment engagement should look the same.

Perhaps the better question for 2027 isn't "do we need a recruiter?" 

It's "what problem are we actually trying to solve and what's the smartest way to solve it?"

Not every problem needs an LLM. And not every problem can be solved without one. ⚖️

Right now it's tempting to throw a large language model at everything. But after seeing both approaches in practice, I think the real skill is knowing which tool fits which problem.

⚙️ Where specialized algorithms win:
Route optimization, scheduling, fraud scoring, search ranking, inventory forecasting. These problems have clear rules and measurable goals. A well-tuned algorithm gives you speed (milliseconds, not seconds), predictable results, low cost at scale, and outputs you can explain and audit. An LLM solving a shortest-path problem is like hiring a poet to do your accounting.

🧠 Where LLMs win:
Messy, unstructured, language-heavy tasks: summarizing documents, answering customer questions, drafting content, extracting meaning from emails or contracts. Writing rules for these by hand is nearly impossible, and LLMs handle the ambiguity remarkably well.

📊 The trade-offs in short:
Specialized algorithms are fast, cheap, precise, and explainable, but rigid and costly to build for each new problem.
LLMs are flexible, quick to prototype, and great with language, but slower, more expensive per request, and sometimes confidently wrong.

🔗 The best solutions often combine both. Let the LLM understand the request ("find me the cheapest delivery plan for these orders"), then hand the actual computation to a proven algorithm. The LLM becomes the interface; the algorithm does the heavy lifting.

The question isn't "algorithm or AI?" It's "what does this problem actually need?"

Have you seen a case where an LLM was overkill, or where it replaced a system that was hard to maintain? 👇

This is a follow-up to my previous post on moving beyond FTE as I ran out of room for tactical advice. Some is from my own experience, but most is from advice I'd received that resonated.

1. Do your basic career stuff.

Update your LinkedIn. There are gig marketplaces out there, but LinkedIn still seems to be the main platform for folks to figure out what you're all about. Make sure someone who doesn't already know you can understand what you're good at.

Update your resume to address 3 audiences: AI screening you in/out, the recruiter checking your experience, and the hiring manager looking at your impact. Use relevant language (take a peek at job postings) to be discoverable while still telling a compelling story to an actual human.

Apply before you feel qualified. I'm especially talking to women here. If you can do the core work and have evidence that you can learn the rest, consider applying and let them decide whether you're qualified.

2. Get comfortable talking about yourself.

Take recruiter calls. If a recruiter reaches out consider having the conversation, even if you're unsure about the job. It's practice talking about your experience, compensation, and what you're looking for. And gives you another person you can check in with periodically.

Be consultative instead of salesy or beggy. Reaching out to folks was something I struggled with initially because I worried it would feel transactional. Someone advised me to think about these conversations as a win-win instead. Ask people what they're working on and only offer help when you can. You don't have to enter every conversation trying to get something from it.

Don't only search for 'fractional/part-time.' Try terms like contract, consultant, project-based, interim, temporary, vendor, etc. And listen for problems, not just job titles. If you find your own gig, you can start your own company or find a staffing company to work through. They'll take a cut, but in return they can handle the paperwork.

3. Allow yourself to experiment and pivot.

Figure out what someone will pay you for. What do you want to do? What problems have you solved repeatedly?

Have an elevator pitch. This is one I'm still working on now that my title and employer stopped explaining for me. 'I'm a resourceful generalist who can figure out a lot of things' (see? a WIP). You don't need the perfect elevator pitch, but you should probably have something so you don't ramble like I do.

Be prepared for the money to be weird. I don't know how soon it becomes predictably lucrative. You may take a pay cut. Benefits matter. Taxes matter. Business development takes time.

It's a big world out there. I didn't leave corp or tech entirely as I now consult for corporate clients, so I'm a bit of an imposter writing this. But I've talked with friends who went on to do things completely different and love it.

There are entire worlds outside the career-path bubble many of us have been in.
And I find that thrilling.

Microsoft just told on itself.

Not on purpose. But its Copilot redesign this week says the quiet part out loud: three pieces now, Home, Code and Autopilot. Home is where you chat and collaborate. Code builds software. Autopilot is the one that matters here. It does not assist a person doing a task. It runs the task, persistently, without anyone opening a window to ask it to.

Ronald Coase answered the question underneath this in 1937, long before software existed. A company decides where its walls end by comparing two costs: what it costs to coordinate work inside the building versus what it costs to buy that same work from the outside market. For thirty years the outsourcing industry lived on the "buy" side of that line. Not because in-house was impossible. Because coordinating a process internally, hiring for it, training it, managing its quality, absorbing its turnover, cost more than sending the seat somewhere it was cheaper to run.

Autopilot is a bet that internal coordination cost is about to fall toward zero. If an agent inside your own stack can run the process end to end, the math that justified "buy" for three decades starts to move.

The same week, Anthropic signed a seven year, $11.6 billion cloud contract with Akamai Technologies, plus warrants for up to 5% of Akamai's stock. Even the labs building the agents are rewriting their own make or buy math, in real time, with real money.

Here is what none of this changes. I have built delivery operations across 18 countries. The vendors who last the next five years were never selling headcount. They were selling judgment: which exception needs escalation, which client meant something different than what they typed, which regulatory quirk in one country breaks a workflow that runs fine everywhere else. No agent ships with that built in. Someone still has to build it, train it and own the outcome when it is wrong.

AI does not fix a flawed process. It accelerates the exposure of one.

So the real question for anyone buying outsourced services right now is not whether AI replaces the vendor. It is whether you were ever paying for a process, or just a discount on headcount.

Which one is your contract?
